segments.narration: Four farmers drained a pond and found a giant room.
Longyou County, Zhejiang, 1992. The village had always called that pond bottomless. They pumped for seventeen straight days.
Under the water: a hand-cut sandstone hall with pillars and a vaulted roof. Twenty-four have now been cleared, ceilings up to thirty metres, thirty thousand square metres of rock removed.
And every single surface wears the same parallel chisel marks, angled the same way, band after band. So who does that and writes nothing down?

Relics inside date to the Han dynasty or earlier. The most concrete answer came in 2014: one researcher argues a defeated king named Goujian hid his army down here, which is why no scribe was ever allowed to mention it.

verdicts.claim: In 1992 four villagers in Longyou County, Zhejiang, drained a pond and found a large man-made cavern beneath it.
verdicts.note: 83% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)

verdicts.claim: The villagers pumped for 17 days to empty a pond locals believed was bottomless.
verdicts.note: The 17-day pumping figure and the 'bottomless pond' local belief come from the site operator's own account of the discovery.

verdicts.claim: Twenty-four artificial sandstone caverns have been cleared and studied, with ceilings up to 30 metres and a combined area of over 30,000 square metres.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives 24 caverns, ceilings up to 30 m, over 30,000 square metres combined. The official site notes over 50 caves are known in total with 24 cleared and studied, which is the figure used.

verdicts.claim: Every surface carries parallel chisel marks set at about 60 degrees in bands roughly 60 centimetres wide, and no surviving text records the caves' construction.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives the 60-degree angle and ~60 cm bands and states the construction is not recorded in any historical document; the official site and IFLScience both confirm no surviving text records the project.

verdicts.claim: Relics from the reign of Emperor Xuan of Han (91-48 BCE) were found in the caves, and in 2014 researcher Yang Hongxun proposed they were dug around 494 BC to hide King Goujian's soldiers.
verdicts.note: IFLScience reports both the Emperor Xuan relics and Yang Hongxun's 2014 Goujian proposal. It is one researcher's hypothesis, not a settled finding — the narration presents it as one researcher's argument, and the sources agree no explanation has answered every question.
